So Why Aren’t They Using Your Product? Auxle 6 min read · Just now -- Listen Share Getting someone to create an account is one thing. Getting them to come back is a completely different sport. You launch your product. You share it on LinkedIn. Post about it on X. Send it to friends. Maybe even convince a few people to try it. Then the sign-ups start coming in. Five. Ten. Twenty. You refresh the dashboard. Thirty! For a brief moment, you feel like you’ve cracked the internet. Then you check again the next day. Nothing. The users who signed up yesterday haven’t returned. Some haven’t even completed their profiles. One person created an account, looked around for 14 seconds, and disappeared forever. You check the analytics again. Maybe the tracking is broken? Nope. The tracking is fine. Your users have simply moved on with their lives. Welcome to one of the most uncomfortable parts of building a product: people signing up doesn’t necessarily mean they want to use it. A sign-up is a hello, not a commitment It’s easy to get excited about registrations. Sign-ups are visible. They go up. They look good in a screenshot. You can tell your friends that 100 people have joined your platform. But what happens after they sign up? Did they complete the onboarding? Did they try the main feature? Did they get anything useful out of the product? Did they come back the next day? These questions matter much more than the registration count. Imagine building a project management tool. Someone signs up, creates a workspace, looks at the dashboard, and leaves. Technically, that’s a new user. But did they actually experience the product’s value? Not really. They just visited your digital property, had a look around, and left without even using the facilities. Your onboarding might be the problem Here’s something founders often underestimate: Users don’t arrive with your product roadmap in their heads. You know exactly what your product does. You know why you built that feature, where everything lives, and why the settings page has 14 options. Your new user knows absolutely none of that. They’ve just landed on your website and are trying to figure out what to do next. If the first experience involves five forms, three verification steps, a profile setup, and a tutorial that feels longer than a university orientation programme, you’ve got a problem. Good onboarding shouldn’t teach users everything. It should help them reach their first useful outcome. For example: A project management tool should help users create their first project. A design tool should help users create something. An analytics platform should help users understand their first useful insight. A networking platform should help users discover a relevant connection. The goal is simple: get users to experience the reason they signed up in the first place. Don’t make them work too hard to find it. Time-to-value: how long before users say “Oh, this is useful”? There’s a useful concept in product development called time-to-value . In simple terms, it’s the time between someone starting to use your product and experiencing its first meaningful benefit. And it’s worth paying attention to. Imagine two products. Product A: Sign up. Verify email. Complete your profile. Select preferences. Watch an introduction. Configure settings. Finally, use the product. Product B: Sign up. Try the main feature. Get something useful. Which one gives the user a reason to return? Of course, some products genuinely require setup. You can’t remove every step just to make onboarding shorter. But every additional step should have a purpose. If users need to complete ten actions before seeing any value, ask yourself whether all ten are really necessary. Sometimes the best onboarding improvement isn’t adding another tutorial. It’s removing three unnecessary steps. Stop guessing. Start looking at user behaviour. When users aren’t returning, founders often jump straight into building new features. “Maybe users need notifications.” “Maybe we should add AI.” “Maybe a dashboard redesign will fix everything.” And suddenly, the product has six new features, but the original problem is still sitting there, enjoying the view. Before adding anything, look at what users are actually doing. Start with a simple funnel: Visited: Did they reach your product? Signed up: Did they create an account? Activated: Did they complete the main action? Returned: Did they come back? Retained: Did they continue using it over time? This helps you identify where people are dropping off. For example: Lots of visitors but few sign-ups? Your value proposition or landing page might need work. Lots of sign-ups but few activated users? Look at onboarding and the first experience. Lots of activated users but few returning? Maybe the product isn’t providing enough ongoing value. Users return but don’t pay? Look at your pricing, packaging, and whether the paid features solve a meaningful problem. These are different problems. They shouldn’t all be solved by adding another feature. Talk to the people who left Your analytics can tell you what happened. They usually can’t tell you why. And sometimes, the best product insight comes from asking someone a very simple question: “Hey, I noticed you tried the product. Was there anything that made you stop using it?” That’s it. No 20-question survey. No car
